21 A rectangular block of steel supporting a very large component of a bridge has a height of 15 cm
and a cross-section of 20 cm × 12 cm. It is designed to compress 1 mm when under maximum,
evenly distributed, load.
The Young modulus of steel is 2.0 × 1011
N m–2.
What is the maximum load it can support?
A
32 MN
B
56 GN
C
720 GN
D
32 TN

hints: Notice the three lengths in the block question: original height $15 \text{ cm}$, cross-section $20 \text{ cm} \times 12 \text{ cm}$, and compression $1 \text{ mm}$ - all must be in metres before using $E$ in $\text{N m}^{-2}$.
Connect the compression to Young modulus with $E = \text{stress}/\text{strain} = (F/A)/(x/L)$, where $x = 1 \text{ mm}$ and $L = 15 \text{ cm}$.
Rearrange to $F = EAx/L$, substitute $E = 2.0 \times 10^{11} \text{ N m}^{-2}$, $A = 0.20 \times 0.12 \text{ m}^2$ and $x/L = 0.001/0.15$, then express the newtons in MN.
walkthrough: Convert all lengths to SI units: $L = 15 \text{ cm} = 0.15 \text{ m}$, sides $0.20 \text{ m}$ and $0.12 \text{ m}$, and extension $x = 1 \text{ mm} = 0.001 \text{ m}$.
Convert stress to force: $F = \text{stress} \times A = 1.33 \times 10^9 \times 0.024 = 3.2 \times 10^7 \text{ N}$.
Check units and prefix: $3.2 \times 10^7 \text{ N} = 32 \times 10^6 \text{ N} = 32 \text{ MN}$. This is option A.

A.explanation: Using $F = EAx/L$ gives about $3.2 \times 10^7 \text{ N} = 32 \text{ MN}$.

B.explanation: 56 GN is far too large and does not follow from $E = 2.0 \times 10^{11} \text{ N m}^{-2}$ with $A = 0.024 \text{ m}^2$ and strain $0.001/0.15$.

C.explanation: 720 GN is far too large, consistent with failing to convert cm and mm to m when finding stress and strain.

D.explanation: 32 TN equals $3.2 \times 10^{13} \text{ N}$, a factor of $10^6$ larger than the correct force, from a power-of-ten error in area or extension.
